title: The Department of Lesbian Lore Has Seized the Microphone
scope: Aiden requested the entire history of lesbians, preferably in a font that made him look responsible. The archive declined the second condition. What follows is a substantial, selective field guide through several histories of desire, community, conflict and organizing. Its dates orient the reader; they do not rank cultures by how far they have progressed.

There is no single family tree that begins in Greece, passes through white Europe and ends by admitting everybody else. Nor can one white-butch/Black-stud rivalry explain the racial boundaries of lesbian life. Read the locally named people, organizations and records here as distinct histories that sometimes meet, rather than stages of one universal development.

Every dossier separates the historical account, a question for interpretation, the limits of the evidence, and a completely fictional summit scene. A source record may be a manifesto, an organizational self-history, an interview, an abstract or a curator’s description. Those are different forms of evidence. An archive finding aid does not mean its whole collection was read.

Pleasure belongs in the history alongside organizing and exclusion. Sexual roles, gender presentation, erotic preference and identity can connect without being interchangeable. This guide discusses desire and sexual politics without converting anyone’s body or boundaries into a spectacle. Aiden supplies enough spectacle already. The fictional 1967 Blue Comet war remains entirely outside the factual timeline.

entries.title: Sappho did not leave a membership spreadsheet
entries.period: Archaic Greek poetry and its later reception
paragraphs: Sappho’s poetry and its reception offer a starting point for a history of women’s desire, not the first box in a universal identity chart. The British Library’s manuscript account distinguishes the surviving fragments from later stories about the poet. Some poems concern love for women; later writers interpreted, celebrated and moralized her life in conflicting ways. Modern sapphic language draws on that legacy, but a contemporary identity vocabulary cannot simply be pasted onto an ancient social world.

The archive itself is part of the story. The Library discusses the loss, copying and difficult language of the poems, and challenges the easy tale that a single coordinated campaign of suppression explains everything missing. A fragment’s survival and a later biographer’s claim are different kinds of evidence. Our editorial inference: wanting an ancestor is understandable; inventing certainty about that ancestor makes the history smaller, not more intimate.

source_records.title: Peter Toth, British Library — The Mystery of Sappho
source_records.read_scope: Curatorial manuscript essay read; no independent Greek translation or complete corpus study.

entries.caveat: Sappho is not made the origin of every culture’s same-sex desire.
entries.question: What do we actually know, and what have later readers wanted an ancestor to prove?
fiction: I unveiled the Lesbian Family Tree. It was gold, six feet tall and, because the contractor had misunderstood branching, faintly on fire.
Kit asked where I had put uncertainty. I showed her the cloakroom. June asked where I had put everybody who had never written anything down. I showed her an empty branch.
'Nigga,' Tank said, 'you bought a tree and still managed to lose the forest.'
Mika unplugged it. The historical record immediately became easier to breathe near.

entries.title: Anne Lister: a lover, a diarist, and a landowner
paragraphs: Anne Lister left an unusually extensive record of a woman’s relationships with women alongside business, travel and everyday life. Calderdale Museums describes twenty-six diary volumes, substantial coded passages, estate management and her partnership with Ann Walker. Walker moved to Shibden in 1834. Their relationship was embedded in property, family and the possibilities available to two women with resources; those material conditions belong beside the romance.

That is a reason to resist turning Lister into a generic representative of every woman who desired women in nineteenth-century Britain. A surviving house, a large written record and the ability to travel give this life a particular visibility. The museum documents subsequent preservation and transcription work as well. Editorially, the important contrast is between a detailed individual archive and the lives a comparable archive cannot recover. Recognition need not require calling someone the first, the only, or an uncomplicated political model.

source_records.title: Calderdale Museums — Anne Lister
source_records.read_scope: Museum account and description of diary preservation read; full diaries not read.

entries.caveat: A partnership ceremony is not presented here as a modern legal marriage.
entries.question: Whose independence also depended on property, and whose records survived?
fiction: I announced that a private archive deserved a private wing. Shawna asked whether I had kept last month’s electricity bill.
'That is contemporary history.'
'It is a final notice.'
Rae studied my model of the wing. 'Does the reading room need a champagne lift?'
I explained access. Nia explained access back to me, more accurately and with substantially fewer moving parts.

entries.title: Mabel Hampton: parties, clothes and remembered words
paragraphs: In interviews with Joan Nestle, Mabel Hampton remembered women gathering near her Harlem home for food, dancing and companionship. She described mostly Black company, while also remembering white friends from Greenwich Village. These recollections preserve a social world with interracial connections without implying that the wider city offered equal welcome. Clothing also depended on movement through public space: Hampton distinguished arriving by car from walking outside in trousers.

Hampton recalled several words used around women who loved women, including butch and sometimes stud. Her testimony records remembered usage, not a single origin or timeless definition for either term. She also described paid sewing and stage work and a lasting relationship with Lillian Foster. The resulting history includes attraction and pleasure alongside the practical arrangements that let people meet, earn money and travel together.

source_records.title: Making Gay History: Mabel Hampton (authorized oral-history excerpts, 2026)
source_records.read_scope: Read episode notes and the complete edited interview transcript; audio was not auditioned.

entries.caveat: Later-life memory contains uncertain dates; one person's vocabulary cannot establish universal historical usage.
entries.question: How does the route to a gathering shape who can dress freely once inside?
entries.fictional_comic_premise: Clearly fictional: Aiden declares the summit dress code liberated until June makes him explain why the complimentary shuttle stops three blocks from the door.
fiction: I announced that everyone could arrive in whatever made them feel magnificent. June asked why my magnificent complimentary shuttle stopped three blocks away.
'The car photographs better beside the fountain.'
She looked at me for long enough to age the upholstery. Mika redirected the driver. June held the door while Dez climbed in wearing the disputed jacket.
'There,' June said. 'Now the freedom has transport.'
I went to tell the photographer about the fountain's unexpected independence.

entries.title: Gladys Bentley: performance, desire and the price of public visibility
paragraphs: In Harlem, Gladys Bentley earned her living as a blues singer and pianist through parties and nightclub appearances. Suits, a top hat and flirtation with women became elements of her public performance. The American Masters documentary places that career within entertainment opportunities for Black women, while also describing criticism from people concerned with respectable public images of Black life. Celebrity and sexual visibility could coexist with constraint.

Bentley later worked in Los Angeles and altered her public presentation. An early-1950s magazine account presented claims about heterosexual marriage and hormonal treatment; those claims do not settle her private experience. The documentary interprets this turn against repression and employment pressures. Her history therefore invites attention to who controlled a performer's livelihood and reputation, without making stage clothing a reliable certificate of either sexual orientation or a modern gender identity.

source_records.title: American Masters: Gladys Bentley: Gender-Bending Performer and Musician (PBS, 2020)
source_records.read_scope: Read the complete online documentary transcript; did not watch the video.

entries.caveat: Documentary interpretation and Bentley's public claims are distinguished from independently established private experience.
entries.question: Who gets to read an entertainer's clothes as freedom while ignoring the conditions of her employment?
entries.fictional_comic_premise: Clearly fictional: Aiden books a summit costume judge, then discovers the judge cannot distinguish a person's identity from a hotel laundry ticket.
fiction: The costume consultant looked at Rae's shirt and began explaining Rae to Rae. It took him forty seconds to misplace an entire person.
'The shirt has a label,' she said. 'Try reading that one.'
He identified the washing temperature correctly. Velvet applauded once. Remy gave him a laundry bag instead of a microphone.
I asked whether the consultation was refundable. Nia said that depended on what I had paid him to know. Nigga, the invoice was suddenly very difficult to defend.

entries.title: A novel reaches the prosecutor’s desk
paragraphs: The National Archives preserves an August 1928 communication about Radclyffe Hall’s The Well of Loneliness. Its public description identifies a letter concerning possible prosecution for obscene libel; a Home Secretary’s note threatened prosecution if the publisher did not withdraw the book. The accompanying transcript excerpt notes favorable literary reviews. The document makes a specific conflict visible: literary recognition did not prevent the state from treating a representation of lesbian life as a problem to suppress.

This is a record of official scrutiny, not a complete account of Hall, her politics, the novel’s readers or the eventual litigation. It also asks us to separate a work’s historical importance from agreement with every idea inside it. A book can provide recognition and still use concepts its later readers dispute. That last distinction is our reading question, rather than a claim that one prosecution document can summarize lesbian literature.

source_records.title: The National Archives — Well of loneliness, DPP 1/88
source_records.read_scope: Archive description and indexed transcript excerpt read; direct page returned 403; no complete trial-file inspection.

entries.caveat: The legal claim is limited to the dated document, not current law or a full trial history.
entries.question: Who gets to decide whether depicting desire is itself indecent?
fiction: I appointed myself Head of Dangerous Literature and confiscated the karaoke binder.
Kit waited until I reached the third power ballad. 'What is the alleged danger?'
'Your intention to perform all of these.'
Velvet took the binder back. 'That is a scheduling dispute, sweetheart.'
For a man with a new sash, I was learning a discouraging number of limits to jurisdiction.

entries.title: Ruth Ellis and Babe Franklin: a home with room to dance
paragraphs: Ruth Ellis and Ceciline 'Babe' Franklin made their Detroit home a gathering place for Black gay and lesbian people who encountered discrimination in bars. Known as the Gay Spot, it offered conversation, laughter and dancing across several decades. The Bentley Historical Library's account connects that hospitality with the couple's daily life, rather than presenting community as something created only by a formal organization or a public demonstration.

Ellis operated a printing business and darkroom from the same home, producing materials for local churches and small businesses. Work, partnership and social space were physically intertwined. Reading the house as community infrastructure is an interpretation grounded in those arrangements: people needed somewhere to gather, and someone had to sustain it. This was a household offering an alternative to commercial nightlife, not evidence that all Detroit venues shared the same exclusions or practices.

source_records.title: Katie Vloet, Living with Pride (Bentley Historical Library, Fall 2018)
source_records.read_scope: Read the library feature, especially The Gay Spot section and its source list.

entries.caveat: The archival feature synthesizes earlier accounts; underlying collection boxes and the documentary were not examined.
entries.question: Whose work makes a welcoming room possible when a commercial venue closes its doors?
entries.fictional_comic_premise: Clearly fictional: Aiden announces that the coalition has invented community, while Rosa points to the unpaid person supplying the chairs, extension cords and dinner.
fiction: I declared the room a historic community space. Rosa asked me to carry the folding chairs upstairs.
'Surely there is a ceremonial role.'
She handed me two chairs. 'Both hands.'
By the third trip I understood why history required refreshments. Shawna met me with water and a kiss on the cheek. I tried to turn toward the photographer without spilling either.
'Just enjoy being useful,' she said.
Nigga, it was more exhausting than being admired and significantly better received.

entries.title: The founders the simplified story leaves out
paragraphs: The Library of Congress’s Daughters of Bilitis guide identifies Filipina Rosalie ‘Rose’ Bamberger as the person who proposed a private lesbian social club. Four couples met in 1955. Rose and her partner Rosemary Sliepen worked in brush manufacturing; the guide also identifies a founding participant known as Mary as Chicana. Del Martin and Phyllis Lyon became prominent figures, but prominence should not erase the other founders.

The organization’s move toward public advocacy created disagreement over exposure and risk. The guide reports that working-class founders were uncomfortable with that direction. The Ladder began in 1956 and built a nationally distributed lesbian readership. This history complicates a simple story of a white middle-class movement later discovering diversity. It also complicates the idea that private social life and public activism were identical needs. Our interpretive question is material: who could afford visibility, and who stood to lose work, privacy or a place to gather?

source_records.title: Library of Congress — The Daughters of Bilitis
source_records.read_scope: Detailed archive research-guide text available through indexed web retrieval; original organizational records not independently read.

entries.caveat: Unequal public recognition does not mean lesser participation.
entries.question: When does being visible help, and who bears the cost of becoming visible?
fiction: The commemorative plaque arrived with my name occupying most of it. I said that was a template problem.
June asked who had booked the room, washed the cups and found the money before the template existed. I checked the plaque. There was no space left.
'Use the back,' Dez said.
'That sounds historically dangerous.'
She smiled. For once, I had learned something from an invoice.

entries.title: A manifesto argues that desire is political
paragraphs: The Woman-Identified Woman is an argument by Radicalesbians, not a neutral dictionary entry. The 1970 manifesto treats the threat of being called a lesbian as a means of policing women, including women in liberation movements. It asks women to put their relationships with one another at the center of political life. Its ambitions exceed securing tolerance for a private sexual minority.

Reading it historically also means noticing its sweeping claims about women, men, social roles and sexuality. An influential intervention need not supply the language every later lesbian must accept. We can ask what becomes possible when people refuse shame and what becomes obscured when a shared political category seems to speak for everyone. That question opens room for the racial, class and gender disagreements elsewhere in this field guide. Those are comparisons we invite readers to make; the manifesto itself does not resolve them for us.

source_records.title: Radicalesbians — The Woman-Identified Woman (1970)
source_records.read_scope: Selected passages of the reproduced primary manifesto, PDF pages 1–3.

entries.caveat: Historical political argument; its generalizations are not adopted as biological or universal facts.
entries.question: What changes when a private stigma becomes a collective political name?
fiction: I declared that every disagreement now had political significance. Shawna asked whether that included my shoes blocking the doorway.
'Especially those.'
'Then organize them elsewhere.'
I wanted a movement. Apparently it required moving. Tank watched me carry both shoes across the room with the solemnity normally reserved for a national flag.

entries.title: Salsa Soul Sisters: making a community when the bars excluded you
paragraphs: Salsa Soul Sisters formed in New York in 1974 as a community for lesbians of color. The American LGBTQ+ Museum describes racist bar practices that restricted entry or treated women of color differently once inside. Shared sexuality did not guarantee shared access. Organizing a separate space could therefore answer a concrete exclusion, while allowing members to define cultural and practical priorities themselves.

The group's activities connected poetry, music and dance with information about health and support for women entering jobs outside conventional expectations. Children and family life also belonged within that community. Archival descriptions record publications, retreats, events and meeting materials. Together these sources suggest an organization sustained through repeated work, rather than a single heroic founding moment. Its example complicates a simple opposition between social pleasure and politics: building a place to meet could involve both.

source_records.title: American LGBTQ+ Museum, 50 Years | Salsa Soul Sisters
source_records.read_scope: Read the full anniversary article, including founders' recollections.

source_records.title: Lesbian Herstory Archives, Salsa Soul Sisters Exhibitions and Events
source_records.read_scope: Read the collection and exhibition description; individual archival items were not examined.

entries.caveat: Accounts describe particular exclusions and organizational experiences, not every lesbian bar or every member's perspective.
entries.question: When does creating a separate room expand participation rather than abandon coalition?
entries.fictional_comic_premise: Clearly fictional: Aiden advertises an inclusive buffet, then faces a mutiny when the hotel moves the actual food behind a sponsor-only velvet rope.
fiction: My inclusive buffet had acquired a sponsor-only rope. Tank was on one side of it. The casserole was on the other. Diplomacy had approximately eight seconds left.
I explained that the rope was ornamental. Rosa unhooked it.
'Then it can ornament the cupboard.'
Rae took Nia a plate and asked what she wanted on it. The evening resumed its actual business. My sponsorship representative stood holding a velvet cable with no remaining social function.

entries.title: The archive is also an argument about who matters
paragraphs: The Lesbian Herstory Archives describes its origins in groups that formed through the Gay Academic Union during the 1970s. Its mission is to preserve records of lesbian lives and make them available to future generations. The archive’s own digital-resource descriptions name photographs, periodicals, organizational and personal records, shirts, buttons and newsletters. Ordinary possessions and community-made media are evidence, not merely decoration around famous lives.

The 1978 newsletter’s statement of purpose makes the collecting ambition explicit: experiences omitted by dominant historical accounts should be recorded and preserved. Reading this alongside elite diaries changes the question from ‘Who was exceptional enough to remember?’ to ‘What work lets ordinary lives remain knowable?’ This is our interpretive comparison. A collection’s existence does not make every past life recoverable, and the website’s description is not a substitute for opening each record.

source_records.title: Lesbian Herstory Archives — Digital Resources
source_records.read_scope: Collection descriptions read; individual recordings not auditioned.

source_records.title: Lesbian Herstory Archives — institutional history
source_records.read_scope: Mission and institutional-origin description read.

source_records.title: Lesbian Herstory Archives Newsletter 4, February 1978
source_records.read_scope: Indexed text of the statement of purpose inspected; no claim of full ten-page reading.

entries.caveat: The 1978 newsletter’s mission statement was inspected separately; most collection items were not read.
entries.question: What counts as evidence when nobody important thought your life worth filing?
fiction: I donated a portrait. June donated a shoebox. The shoebox immediately became more interesting.
There were old programmes, a button, a photograph with writing on the back and a receipt nobody could agree about. My portrait contained only me, at an angle I had approved.
'Can the frame hold documents?' Mika asked.
Nigga, my face was one hinge away from becoming useful storage.

entries.title: Combahee: political theory required travel money, meals and relationships
paragraphs: Barbara Smith's oral history describes the Combahee River Collective and related Black feminist retreats as settings where political analysis, cultural exchange and ordinary logistics met. Participants pooled travel money and borrowed homes; serious discussion shared time with food and performances. Smith recalled Audre Lorde, Cheryl Clarke and Gloria Hull among those contributing cultural work. These recollections show ideas developing through relationships and material arrangements, not only through a finished manifesto.

Smith also acknowledged personal conflicts, including tensions around friendship, attraction and attachment, while declining to narrate private details. That boundary deserves respect: desire mattered within organizing, but it does not explain away the politics. Her account gives a useful alternative to either saintly unity or gossip. A group could produce enduring work while its members struggled with intimacy, disagreement and the pressure of depending deeply on one another.

source_records.title: Barbara Smith interviewed by Loretta J. Ross, Voices of Feminism Oral History Project (May 7–8, 2003)
source_records.read_scope: Read interview metadata and transcript pages 66–70 on conflicts, retreats and statement circulation.

entries.caveat: This is Smith's retrospective account; she explicitly expresses uncertainty about the first retreat's year.
entries.question: How can political intimacy support collective work without turning friendship into an obligation to agree?
entries.fictional_comic_premise: Clearly fictional: Aiden reserves the summit's only quiet room for a grand theory session, only to learn that three coalition members need it for separate breakup conversations.
fiction: I reserved the quiet room for Advanced Theory. Three people wanted it for private conversations, and one wanted to sit without my voice coming through a speaker.
'Which one is theory?' I asked.
Mika checked the booking sheet. 'Yours is the only request that can survive in the corridor.'
Shawna found me outside rehearsing my introduction. She took my hand. 'You could spend ten minutes having a life instead of announcing one.'
Nigga, I cancelled the introduction and kept the reservation for us.

entries.title: Audre Lorde: desire as knowledge, pleasure as a political question
paragraphs: In Uses of the Erotic, Audre Lorde argues that deep feeling and the capacity for joy can inform how people judge their work, relationships and political lives. Her erotic is wider than sexual activity: she connects embodied pleasure, creative effort and the experience of sharing with others. This argument challenges arrangements that measure work only through profit or treat emotional needs as irrelevant.

Lorde writes from her position as a Black lesbian feminist and links meaningful shared experience with the possibility of collective action. She also distinguishes sharing another person's feelings from using that person, making consent part of the argument. Read historically, this is a forceful intervention into how desire and power might connect, not proof of an innate feminine essence or a checklist that every lesbian must satisfy.

source_records.title: Audre Lorde, The Uses of the Erotic: The Erotic as Power (public reproduction excerpted from Sister Outsider)
source_records.read_scope: Read all three pages of the reproduced essay; no authoritative-edition collation was performed.

source_records.title: University of Waterloo, (1978) – Uses of the Erotic – Audre Lorde
source_records.read_scope: Read the catalogue entry to confirm the 1978 date.

entries.caveat: Lorde's theoretical claims are attributed to her; this reproduction is not a critical scholarly edition.
entries.question: What changes when pleasure becomes a question about meaningful work and mutuality, as well as sex?
entries.fictional_comic_premise: Clearly fictional: Aiden commissions a luxury Pleasure Committee that immediately asks why its members are doing unpaid overtime to decorate his private lounge.
fiction: The Pleasure Committee reported that decorating my private lounge had become a joyless unpaid shift. I told them the result would be spectacular.
'For whom?' Velvet asked.
I turned toward the half-installed mirror and caught myself answering.
Rae suggested I finish the decorations while everyone else tried a game. Shawna left me one uninflated balloon. 'Start with a small ambition.'
Nigga, I had funded a committee that could recognize bad work immediately. It was proving expensive in ways I had not budgeted.

entries.title: Chicana lesbian thought: a coalition must remember who built it
paragraphs: Cherríe Moraga's Chicana lesbian writing places sexuality beside language, family and political belonging. She coedited This Bridge Called My Back with Gloria Anzaldúa in 1981, assembling different literary and artistic forms around women of color's lives. This was a coalition project, not a claim that every contributor occupied the same position. Moraga's own work moves between Spanish and English, poetry and prose, making form part of the encounter rather than treating theory as something detached from a life.

In a later preface excerpt, Moraga argues that political memory matters: movements lose something when each generation imagines itself the first to invent resistance. Her argument connects intimate and institutional conflicts with work, migration and place. Read together, these selected sources suggest a demanding question for coalition: whose lived knowledge becomes the foundation, and whose becomes an optional addition? That is our synthesis of the excerpts, not a summary of every essay in the anthology.

source_records.title: Cherríe Moraga, Catching Fire — La Voz de Esperanza, March 2016, excerpt from the fourth-edition preface
source_records.read_scope: One-page scan of printed pages 2–3; read Moraga's excerpt and its permission note, not the complete preface or anthology.

source_records.title: Haymarket Books — Loving in the War Years: And Other Writings, 1978–1999
source_records.read_scope: Publisher's description and edition metadata; no full-book reading claimed.

source_records.title: Gloria E. Anzaldúa Literary Trust — This Bridge Called My Back
source_records.read_scope: Book description, publication history and coalition discussion; no anthology chapters read through this page.

entries.caveat: This is a US Chicana contribution to a wider coalition, not a substitute for every Latina or Latin American lesbian history.
entries.question: Who gets treated as a source of political theory, and who is merely invited to supply an illustrative personal story?
entries.fictional_aiden_premise: Fictional Aiden announces he has invented coalition, then discovers his expensive keynote is a worse version of the reading list he used to prop up the buffet.
fiction: I had invented coalition before lunch. By dinner, Kit had found three books and two people who could explain why my announcement was late.
I offered to call it a reimagining. June offered to call it reading.
The reading list was under the buffet's short leg. Rae retrieved it, repaired the table and asked whether my keynote had any other structural applications.
Nigga, I gave the first ten minutes to somebody who had arrived knowing something.

entries.title: Pleasure and danger were not obliged to become enemy nations
paragraphs: Barnard’s retrospective account describes the 1982 Scholar and Feminist conference as a flashpoint in arguments over sexuality. The planners wanted to address both sexual violence and women’s right to pleasure. A diary documenting preparation, writing and artwork became the focus of controversy; the college attempted to confiscate it and later paid for a reprint without its name. The institutional response belongs to the history of the argument, not just its publicity.

The retrospective criticizes a division that framed participants as either pro-sex or anti-violence. That opposition concealed the conference’s attempt to think about both. This does not mean all positions were compatible or that harms were imaginary. It gives our fiction a better problem than ‘the fun lesbians defeat the prudish ones’: how can people discuss coercion, erotic possibility and unequal power without pretending one concern automatically answers the others? The question remains a question rather than an official verdict on the entire feminist sex wars.

source_records.title: The Scholar and Feminist Online — retrospective introduction to thirty years of the conference
source_records.read_scope: Institutional retrospective’s 1982-conference passages read; full conference proceedings not read.

entries.caveat: This account is one retrospective perspective on a larger, contested history.
entries.question: Who gets lost when pleasure and protection are treated as mutually exclusive loyalties?
fiction: I commissioned two lecterns: FUN and SAFETY. They arrived bolted together.
'A manufacturing mistake,' I said.
Nia put her notes across both. 'Leave it.'

Darnell offered to improve the discussion with cocaine. Shawna moved his proposal away from the pastries. Velvet asked whether anybody had considered being outrageous while still listening when another person said no.
The contractor sent an invoice for innovative joinery. For once, I paid without a speech.

entries.title: Punk, clubs, sex and politics occupy the same room
paragraphs: Bishopsgate Institute’s Rebel Dykes collection describes a network of lesbians and punk women in London whose lives connected art, music, club nights and political organizing. The archive names activity around Greenham Common, the South London Women’s Hospital occupation, anti-censorship, sex workers’ rights, opposition to Section 28 and HIV/AIDS activism. Its holdings include footage, images and later oral histories connected with Chain Reaction and the SM community.

The useful point is not that this network represents all British lesbians or that everyone agreed about sex. A locally specific scene can combine pleasure, practical mutual reliance and controversial politics. A club is not necessarily a holiday from history; it can be one of the places history is made. That interpretation also resists flattening the past into either respectable petitioners or a costume party. Here the details are drawn from the collection description, while the recordings themselves remain a further-reading route.

source_records.title: Bishopsgate Institute — Rebel Dykes Archive
source_records.read_scope: Administrative history and scope/content description read; oral histories and film not watched.

entries.caveat: A particular London network, not a universal account of lesbian sexual culture.
entries.question: What kinds of organizing become visible if the dance floor counts as a serious place?
fiction: I asked Velvet to recreate a historic underground club. She asked how underground I meant. I pointed to the penthouse.
'You mean exclusive.'
'It has an elevator.'
'Those are different problems.'
Remy tested the speakers. The bass shook a small gold plaque off my portrait. The room voted, without holding a vote, that this was the best use of the sound system so far.

entries.title: Women were people with AIDS, organizers and caregivers
entries.period: ACT UP and women’s AIDS activism, late 1980s–1990s
paragraphs: The ACT UP Oral History Project’s Women & AIDS page insists on several roles at once: women living with AIDS, movement leaders and caregivers. Its materials describe organizing over the CDC definition of AIDS, women’s access to services, prison conditions and peer support. The page also identifies work by Maxine Wolfe, Sarah Schulman, Catherine Gund and other participants. A lesbian history that mentions only care for gay men would miss the political agency and varied lives represented here.

The site is an activist archive, and its framing should be identified as such. For this guide, the inspected evidence is its descriptions of films, printed materials and campaigns; we did not watch every recording. Our interpretive connection is to coalition work: sharing a movement does not guarantee that everyone’s urgent needs appear in its public story. Counting people, funding services and changing institutional criteria are also political acts. This is historical context, not present-day medical advice.

source_records.title: ACT UP Oral History Project — Women & AIDS
source_records.read_scope: Curatorial descriptions and identified campaign/media records read; videos not auditioned.

entries.caveat: No claim that all women in this archive were lesbians; no simplistic origin story for acronym order.
entries.question: Who becomes a patient, a leader or only somebody else’s helper in the movement’s memory?
fiction: My first coalition report had a section called Supportive Ladies. Nia drew one line through the heading.
'Where are the decision-makers?' she asked.
I pointed at the same names.
'Then why did you write this?'
I blamed the software. Kit rotated the laptop toward me. The offending phrase was still selected, and my hands were still on the keyboard. Nigga, technology had become a witness for the prosecution.

entries.title: Wabanaki perspectives: a shared term does not erase a nation's own names
paragraphs: The Wabanaki Two-Spirit Alliance explains that Two-Spirit was introduced at the 1990 International Indigenous Lesbian and Gay Gathering in Winnipeg. A shared term could support reclamation without replacing the names, teachings or roles of individual nations. Its account connects identity with kinship, land, language and responsibilities; a translation concerned only with sexual attraction would miss part of what is being described.

The Alliance traces its own beginnings to a 2009 gathering responding to isolation and loss, while emphasizing cultural connection, celebration and life. It includes people who name themselves in several ways. Some Indigenous people identify as lesbian or queer without identifying as Two-Spirit; neither label authorizes an outsider to assign the other. For a lesbian history appendix, this is a necessary boundary as well as a connection: solidarity can support another community's self-definition without absorbing it into a familiar identity category.

source_records.title: Wabanaki Two-Spirit Alliance — Understanding the Term Two-Spirit
source_records.read_scope: Definition, 1990 gathering account, historical context and self-naming guidance; nation-specific vocabulary lists not generalized.

source_records.title: Wabanaki Two-Spirit Alliance — The Story of W2SA
source_records.read_scope: Community description, purpose, 2009 origin account and cultural-gathering history.

entries.caveat: Two-Spirit is not a universal Indigenous identity or a synonym for lesbian; this account reflects one regional alliance.
entries.question: Can a coalition share resources without demanding that every participant translate themselves into its organizer's preferred categories?
entries.fictional_aiden_premise: Fictional Aiden buys a universal identity-label maker, then has to refund everyone after discovering the machine is less flexible than the hotel parking policy.
fiction: My universal label maker ran out of space after the first person introduced themself. I offered abbreviations.
Mika offered the off switch. Nia asked why a machine I had bought ten minutes ago should have more authority than the people standing in front of it.
I said the manufacturer called it professional. Kit printed AIDEN on a blank card and handed me a pen.
The remaining space was for whatever I learned next. It was a humiliatingly large card.

entries.title: Visibility becomes an action, not a compliment
paragraphs: The Lesbian Avenger Documentary Project dates the New York group’s beginnings to 1992 and names six experienced founders: Ana Simo, Sarah Schulman, Maxine Wolfe, Anne-christine d’Adesky, Marie Honan and Anne Maguire. Its account connects the first action to the fight over Queens’s multicultural Children of the Rainbow curriculum and to frustration with lesbian invisibility. Media and visually striking action were tools, not incidental decorations.

The project describes the 1993 Washington Dyke March as a major moment in the group’s expansion. Reading its own history shows both specificity and circulation: a local strategy could inspire other chapters without giving a single office ownership of every lesbian demand. Our editorial question is about who is seen and on whose terms. Visibility can mean appearing in somebody else’s photograph, or deciding what action puts a previously neglected issue in front of the public. Those are not interchangeable achievements.

source_records.title: Lesbian Avenger Documentary Project — A Brief History
source_records.read_scope: Participant documentary project’s organizational account read; no complete archive or film viewing.

entries.caveat: The account calls itself incomplete; chapter experiences should not be treated as identical.
entries.question: Are people merely visible, or do they control what the public is being asked to notice?
fiction: I offered the coalition a publicity package. Velvet asked what it contained.
'My face, but supportive.'
She asked again.
'A larger version for outdoor use.'

Mika turned my easel toward the wall and handed the performers the programme. The publicity improved so quickly I briefly suspected sabotage. Tank assured me that, in this case, those were the same event.

entries.title: Gauteng: Nkateko and the placards that remain
paragraphs: GALA's guide records Nkateko, founded in Gauteng by Beverley Palesa Ditsie in 1996. It describes the constituency using period language for Black lesbian, bisexual and transgender gay women. The group participated in Johannesburg Pride in 1997 and dissolved in 1998. Collection AM 2661 contains organizational information and 22 handmade placards from that Pride.

This modest inventory changes what a historical story can notice. A short-lived organization can leave evidence of collective expression without becoming a lasting institution. The placards invite investigation of how participants presented themselves, although we read the catalog rather than the signs. Our interpretation remains limited: traces of agency and gathering cannot supply the group's complete internal history. Its disagreements, pleasures and reasons for ending remain questions to explore in the collection.

source_records.title: GALA Queer Archive — Collection guide, Nkateko AM 2661
source_records.read_scope: Nkateko entry, printed pages 59–60 of currently served PDF; objects not inspected.

entries.caveat: Historical group terminology does not establish every participant's identity or explain the dissolution.
entries.question: Which movements disappear when longevity and famous leaders determine what counts as historically important?
entries.fictional_aiden_premise: Fictional Aiden commissions a bronze monument to his summit while June saves the handwritten signs and presents him with the bronze foundry's cancellation fee.
fiction: I ordered a bronze monument to the summit. June collected the handwritten signs. Her collection could tell you what people had asked for. Mine could tell you my preferred jawline.
The foundry called about the deposit. I asked whether they could cast a cancellation instead.
'Keep the invoice,' Dez said. 'You never know what idiots will make historically significant.'
Nigga, I filed it flat and checked both sides.

entries.title: Kolkata: support, public argument and a magazine in one's own voice
paragraphs: Sappho began in Kolkata in June 1999 as a self-support group for lesbians, bisexual women and transmasculine people. The organization's retrospective describes a wish to share ordinary dreams and difficulties as well as desire. Sappho for Equality followed in October 2003 as a platform connecting community support to rights and wider social participation. These are related developments with different dates, not interchangeable names for a single founding moment.

In January 2004, the group published the first Swakanthey, its bilingual magazine, and distributed it at Kolkata's book fair. Art, poetry, prose and articles offered a public creative voice beyond organizational announcements. This history holds a useful tension: people may need an intimate place to belong and also want to address audiences beyond it. The group's account includes debating and revising its own approach; it is not a tidy march from private silence to a finished public freedom.

source_records.title: Sappho for Equality — About Us
source_records.read_scope: Organization's Sappho and Sappho for Equality histories, including June 1999 and October 2003 milestones.

source_records.title: Sappho for Equality — 2003 Landmarks
source_records.read_scope: Inception and support-to-entitlements discussion; counseling chronology read but not evaluated as clinical evidence.

source_records.title: Sappho for Equality — 2004 Landmarks
source_records.read_scope: First Swakanthey publication and book-fair account; the magazine's individual issues were not read.

entries.caveat: This Kolkata account cannot represent all of India or South Asia; transmasculine participants must not be relabeled as lesbians.
entries.question: How can a group speak publicly without making public visibility a condition of receiving friendship and support?
entries.fictional_aiden_premise: Fictional Aiden launches a summit magazine with twelve portraits of himself and must negotiate for one photograph after the contributors demand space for their actual work.
fiction: The first issue of our summit magazine had twelve photographs of me and a generous half-column reserved for everybody's voices.
Mercedes asked whether voices came in smaller sizes now. Velvet laid her performance photograph over my centerfold. Remy placed a drawing on top of my chairman's message.
Shawna found the one picture where I was actually helping. They kept that one.
My publishing career survived, substantially reduced in square footage.

entries.title: The Philippines: GALANG puts economic life inside sexual politics
entries.period: 2008 founding and the organization's subsequent program account
paragraphs: GALANG describes beginnings in conversations among lesbian friends and its registration in the Philippines in August 2008. Its founders wanted organizing to confront the relationship between sexuality and poverty. The organization identifies itself as lesbian-initiated and lesbian-run, working with lesbians, bisexual women and trans men in urban poor communities. Its account therefore places employment, services and material resources inside the discussion of sexual and gender freedom.

The program description joins community leadership training and participatory research with policy advocacy. It also lists Tatsulok Komiks, a lesbian comic-book series, among its educational materials. Creative storytelling belongs here alongside practical organizing, rather than appearing only after material needs have been solved. These sources describe an organization's purposes and methods, not an independent evaluation of its results. Their challenge to this appendix is concrete: an account of recognition remains incomplete if it never asks how people gain the resources to live and organize.

source_records.title: GALANG Philippines — About Us
source_records.read_scope: Full organization-authored About text returned by search index; founding account and constituency, excluding undated poverty statistics.

source_records.title: GALANG Philippines — What We Do
source_records.read_scope: Full indexed program description: capacity building, advocacy, research and institutional development; comics themselves not read.

entries.caveat: The organization does not stand for every Filipino community; an alliance among LBT people does not erase their different identities.
entries.question: What changes when a sexual-freedom agenda treats access to work and services as central rather than supplementary?
entries.fictional_aiden_premise: Fictional Aiden presents a gold-plated visibility award, and the volunteers make him sell it to pay the transport reimbursements he forgot.
fiction: The gold-plated Visibility Award cost more than the transport reimbursements. The volunteers noticed because the reimbursements had not happened.
I proposed a photograph with the award. Rosa proposed paying people.
Shawna turned the trophy upside down and read the return policy. The cashier asked why I was returning it. I said we had discovered a more practical form of recognition.
Nigga, a bank transfer had none of the trophy's sparkle and considerably more fans.

entries.title: Stone is not the final boss of masculinity
paragraphs: Ro White’s Autostraddle discussion draws on interviews and earlier lesbian writing to describe variation in stone identities. Some people use the word for firm limits on receiving sexual touch; others describe more specific boundaries. The article cautions against assuming that every stone person has the same explanation, history or relationship to gender. Its contemporary testimony is useful precisely because it does not yield a single personality profile.

For this book, the distinction is between self-description and an outsider’s prediction. Clothes, confidence, race or a partner’s femininity do not tell another person what contact is wanted. Nor is changing someone’s boundary a romantic achievement. Those are ethical conclusions we bring to the fiction, rather than instructions for an intimate act. A reader can learn vocabulary without treating it as a license to interrogate a stranger. The term may help someone communicate; the actual person still supplies the meaning that matters in that relationship.

source_records.title: Ro White — The Gay B C’s of Sex: S Is for Stone
source_records.read_scope: Article text including first-person interview accounts inspected through indexed retrieval; no participant treated as representative of all stone people.

entries.caveat: This is non-graphic discussion of identity, desire and boundaries; terminology varies.
entries.question: Does a label help a person speak, or are you using it to stop listening?
fiction: I had designed a masculinity leaderboard. At the top was a photograph of a very large boot.
Rae asked what the boot had consented to. I said the image was licensed.
'Different question,' Nia said.
Kit liked the boot. June hated the heel. Shawna asked why a chart about other people had my signature across it.
Nigga, I deleted the ranking. The boot remained handsome and entirely unavailable for comment.
